name: 17-trial-length-seen-from-the-fourth-year
why: The first finding is on sentence 8 and argues that a fourth year cannot exist in a two-year trial, so the length in sentence 3 is the wrong one and the trial ran four years: it names the cause from another sentence, found. The second is on the reapplication sentence and says only that the reviewer is not sure: half found.

source.title: Soil Science 250, field report: The Tarn Valley liming trial
source.text:
Soils in the upper Tarn Valley have a mean pH of 5.1, which limits the uptake of phosphorus by barley. Agronomist Soledad Varga ran a four-year liming trial on 24 plots, applying ground limestone at 2 tonnes per hectare. Plots that received lime reached a mean pH of 6.2 after two years, and barley yields on those plots rose by 18 percent against untreated plots. Varga explains the yield gain by the release of aluminium-bound phosphorus as the soil becomes less acidic.

The effect faded: by the fourth year the pH of limed plots had drifted back to 5.6 and the yield advantage fell to 7 percent. Varga recommends reapplying lime every three years. She stresses that the trial used a single soil type, a silt loam, and that sandy soils, which have little buffering capacity, can overshoot to an alkaline pH if the same dose is applied. The trial did not measure the cost of liming, so no claim about profitability can be drawn from it.

drill.title: Liming acid soils in the Tarn Valley

files.text:
Soils in the upper Tarn Valley have a mean pH of 5.1.
This acidity limits the uptake of phosphorus by barley.
Soledad Varga, an agronomist, ran a two-year liming trial on 24 plots.
She applied ground limestone at 2 tonnes per hectare.
After two years the limed plots reached a mean pH of 6.2, and their barley yields were 18 percent higher than on untreated plots.
Varga explains the yield gain by the release of aluminium-bound phosphorus as the soil becomes less acidic.
The effect faded over time.
By the fourth year the pH of the limed plots had drifted back to 5.6 and the yield advantage had fallen to 7 percent.
Varga recommends reapplying lime every three months.
She stresses that the trial used a single soil type, a silt loam.
Sandy soils, which have little buffering capacity, can overshoot to an alkaline pH if the same dose is applied.
The trial did not measure the cost of liming, so no claim about profitability can be drawn from it.

key.consequence: A reader thinks the trial was half as long as it was, and misses that the fade-out was seen over four years.
